summary: Specifies how to handle DHCPv4 options that show up more than once in a message, which happens when an option is longer than the 255-byte limit or is split to use option overloading. It updates RFC 2131.

plainLanguage.summary: A DHCP option is a labelled piece of data, and its label and size each fit in one byte, so a single option can hold at most 255 bytes of data. This RFC says how to cut a longer option into pieces, send them in order, and put them back together on the receiving side.

subtitle: How to split a DHCPv4 option longer than 255 bytes into pieces and glue it back together.

tldr.problem: A DHCPv4 option has a one-byte length, so it holds at most 255 bytes, and options also have to fit into the limited space of the option fields in a packet.
tldr.mechanism: An option may be split into several instances with the same option code, stored in order in an aggregate option buffer; the receiver concatenates all instances of the same code into one option before processing.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 2131 with clear concatenation rules, but senders must be careful because many deployed agents do not implement concatenation.

today: RFC 3396 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2002. It updates RFC 2131, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC warns that many deployed DHCP agents do not implement option concatenation, so a sender has to be careful about splitting options.

sections.title: The Problem with Long Options
sections.content:
DHCP specifies objects called options that are encoded in the DHCPv4 packet to pass information between DHCP protocol agents. Each option is encoded as a one-byte type code, a one-byte length, and a buffer of the number of bytes given by the length, from zero to 255.

Sometimes it is useful to send options longer than 255 bytes. RFC 2131 specifies that when more than one option with a given type code appears in the packet, all such options should be concatenated together, but it does not specify the order in which the concatenation should occur. This document specifies the ordering that DHCP protocol agents MUST use when sending options longer than 255 bytes, and it also defines the method MUST be used for splitting shorter options if the encoding agent needs to do so. DHCP protocol agents MUST use the method whenever they receive a packet containing more than one occurrence of a certain type of option.

The document updates the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol and the DHCP Options and BOOTP vendor extensions documents. It also warns that many currently deployed DHCP protocol agents do not implement option concatenation, so agents should be careful not to transmit split options unless it will not matter if the recipient cannot correctly reassemble the options, or it is certain that the recipient implements concatenation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each option in a DHCP message has a one-byte label and a one-byte size field, so one option can carry at most 255 bytes of data. Longer data has to be sent as several options with the same label, and this RFC fixes the order in which they must be put back together.

sections.title: When to Split an Option
sections.content:
The specification applies when a DHCP agent is encoding a packet containing options where some of them must be broken into parts. That need arises for two reasons. The value of an option may be longer than 255 bytes, in which case the encoding agent MUST follow the algorithm in this document. Or there may not be enough space in the current output buffer for the whole option, but there is space for part of it and space in another output buffer for the rest, in which case the encoding agent MUST either use the algorithm or not send the option at all. The specification also applies whenever an agent has received a packet containing more than one instance of an option of a given type: the agent MUST concatenate those instances in the way the document specifies.

The document divides options into two categories. A concatenation-requiring option is one whose own specification requires the mechanisms of this document, which it does by specifically referencing this document. Every other option is a non-concatenation-requiring option.

An agent SHOULD NOT split an option unless it has no choice, or it knows the peer can properly handle split options. A peer is assumed to handle split options properly if it has provided or requested at least one concatenation-requiring option, or if the administrator of the sending agent has configured it to assume the recipient can concatenate. Some implementors find it easiest to split only concatenation-requiring options and never split the others, which is permissible, but an implementation that supports any concatenation-requiring option MUST be able to concatenate received options for both kinds.

No restrictions apply to concatenation on receipt. Any agent that implements these mechanisms can assume that when it receives two options of the same type it should concatenate them.
sections.plainLanguage: Splitting an option is a last resort, because older DHCP software may not join the pieces back together. The RFC therefore limits splitting to options whose own definition requires it, and to cases where the option simply does not fit in the space left.

sections.title: The Aggregate Option Buffer
sections.content:
DHCP options can be stored in three separate portions of the packet: the optional parameters field, the sname field and the file field. This complicates the description of the splitting mechanism, because there are three separate fields into which split options may be placed. An option that does not fit into one field cannot overlap the boundary into another field, so the encoding agent must break the option into two parts and store one part in each buffer.

To simplify the discussion, the RFC describes an aggregate option buffer, the aggregate of the three buffers. The aggregation is logical only: the buffers MUST appear in the locations in the DHCP packet described by RFC 2131. The aggregate option buffer is made up of the optional parameters field, the file field and the sname field, in that order, which is not the physical ordering of these fields in the packet.

Options MUST NOT be stored in the aggregate option buffer in such a way that they cross either boundary between the three fields. The encoding agent is free to choose to use either or both of the sname and file fields; if it does not use them, they MUST NOT be considered part of the aggregate option buffer.
sections.plainLanguage: A DHCP packet has three places where options can live, and the RFC treats them as one long buffer for the purpose of ordering. The order in that buffer is not the order in the packet, which is why the RFC spells it out.

sections.title: Encoding Agent Behavior
sections.content:
Options can be split on any octet boundary. No split portion of a split option can contain more than 255 octets. The split portions MUST be stored in the aggregate option buffer in sequential order: the first portion first, then the second, and so on. The encoding agent MUST NOT attempt to attach any semantic meaning to where the option is split.

Because the aggregate option buffer does not represent the physical ordering of the packet, an option split into three parts with one part in each possible field puts the first part in the optional parameters field, the second in the file field and the third in the sname field. This keeps the result consistent with Section 4.1 of RFC 2131.

Each split portion MUST be stored in the aggregate option buffer as if it were a normal variable-length option. The length fields of the split portions MUST add up to the total length of the option data, and for any option being split the option code field in each portion MUST be the same.
sections.plainLanguage: A piece of an option is written exactly like a whole option: same label, its own length. The pieces go out in order, each one no bigger than 255 bytes, and the reader joins them back together.

sections.title: Decoding Agent Behavior
sections.content:
When a decoding agent scans an incoming packet's option buffer and finds two or more options with the same option code, it MUST consider them to be split portions of a single option. It MUST treat the contents of that option as one option, reassembled in the order described for the encoding agent.

The decoding agent should ensure that when the option's value is used, any alignment issues particular to the machine architecture it runs on are accounted for, because there is no requirement that the encoding agent align the options in any particular way. There is no semantic meaning to where an option is split: the decoding agent MUST reassemble the parts into a single object and MUST NOT treat each portion as a separate object.
sections.plainLanguage: On the receiving side, options that share a label are put back together into one value before anything else looks at them. The point where the cut was made carries no meaning.

sections.title: A Split Option Example
sections.content:
Consider the Bootfile name option, option code 67, with the value "/diskless/foo". Normally this would be encoded as a single option: the code 67, the length 13, and the thirteen bytes of the value.

If an encoding agent needed to split the option to fit it into the option buffer, it could encode it as two separate options and store them in the aggregate option buffer in that sequence: code 67 with length 7 followed by "/diskle", then code 67 with length 6 followed by "ss/foo". The receiver sees two options with code 67, concatenates the two data portions in order, and recovers the original value.
sections.plainLanguage: The example splits a thirteen-byte boot file name into a seven-byte piece and a six-byte piece. Both pieces carry the same option label, so the receiver joins them back into "/diskless/foo".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC raises no new security issues. Potential exposures to attack in the DHCP protocol are discussed in Section 7 of the DHCP protocol specification and in the document on authentication for DHCP messages.

It notes one wrinkle: the authentication option itself can be split, so implementations must be careful when setting the authentication field to zero, before the message authentication code is generated or verified, since it may be spread across multiple options.
sections.plainLanguage: Splitting options adds no new risk by itself. The one thing to watch is the authentication option, which may be split and has to be zeroed correctly before its checksum is computed.

items.title: Any boundary
items.text: An option may be split on any octet boundary.

items.title: At most 255 octets
items.text: No split portion may contain more than 255 octets.

items.title: Same code
items.text: Every portion carries the same option code.

items.title: In order
items.text: The portions are stored in the aggregate buffer in sequence.

items.title: No meaning
items.text: Nothing may depend on where the split happened.
